#3890. Blizzard hints at console ports for World of Warcraft: Forever - "Play it wherever you want and, at some point, on whatever you want"

After more than two decades dominating the PC MMO battlefield, it sounds like Blizzard Entertainment's taking the idea of a World of Warcraft console port more seriously than ever.

World of Warcraft: Forever's beta seems to have been immensely popular with fans of the series. It's a brand new third version of the iconic multiplayer game that sits alongside WoW's Classic and Retail portions, and it's recaptured many a lapsed Warcraft sicko with tons of good changes, big and small - one of which is controller support for the first time ever.

Speaking to GamesRadar about the decision to keep World of Warcraft: Forever exclusive to PC players, despite now supporting gamepads, vice president and executive producer Holly Longdale hinted that the fantasy game might just make its way to even more devices and players over time.

"What you just described is really what we're after," she told the outlet. "Play it wherever you want and, at some point, on whatever you want. But the first leg of that journey is getting gamepads working really well with World of Warcraft, and we thought Forever was the perfect place to start."

Longdale reckons all gaming platforms might become "more ubiquitous" in the future, as well. She specifically named the Xbox Project Helix, which is said to be a PC-console hybrid device of some kind. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma confirmed the next-gen console can even play your PC games earlier in the year.

"Honestly, we just want to be able to play it anywhere. We've seen people getting it working on the ROG Ally X," Longdale added. "I think just doing some of the work we're doing on gamepad is going to give players a lot of flexibility that I think goes beyond consoles."

World of Warcraft: Forever properly launches on the 4th of November.

Despite struggles in the rest of the Xbox division, Forever's beta was supposedly the "largest" in series history. Elsewhere, Longdale acknowledged that some of the developer's decisions won't make everybody equally happy: "I think the lesson we learned the most over time is 'You don't listen to the loudest people in the room.'"

As for projects still in the works, the proposed timeline slots Creature and Commandos season 2 in between Peacemaker season 2 and Supergirl. "Implemented terminal velocity": great news for Tarhiel.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you are playing Morrowind in 2026, my recommendation is that you do so using OpenMW, its 18-year-old fan-made and open-source engine reimplementation that makes it run smooth as butter on any modern machine you point it at, whether you're running Windows, Linux, macOS or, hell, FreeBSD if you wanna get really sicko with it. It's simply the most convenient way to get a cromulent version of Bethesda's best game running on modern systems.

And now it has a new version. Or rather, a new release candidate that will prove the basis of its upcoming 0.52 version. Released a couple of days ago, OpenMW 0.52 RC1 contains a bunch of fixes, some new features, and one minor alteration to the fundamental forces of the universe. It's not the doozy of, say, OpenMW 0.50—which added gamepad support and thereby made Morrowind on Steam Deck dizzyingly easy—but it's still pretty meaty.

For instance, consider: "Water-walking actors now drown when knocked out" and "Implemented terminal velocity". Say what you like, but the second of those seems pretty meaningful for a game that contains Scrolls of Icarian Flight and the first is quite a funny sentence. The terminal velocity fix contains, within itself, a sub-fix for the basic laws of reality: "fixed gravity being 0.01% off"). We are free of our shared hell.

The biggest new feature in OpenMW 0.52 is probably the lighting stuff. It's called clustered lighting and it removes "the normal per-object light limit". I don't really know what that means either, but the short and tall of it, per an explanatory August blog post, is that "it has a dramatically lower performance impact than raising the limit to Aetherius. In fact, the performance can in some cases be better than with the regular light limit."

Morrowind, one of the best videogames ever made, continues to get better.

#3886. Fix up towering robots while battle rages outside in Bay 12: Mech Repair, a first-person job sim with some handsome heavy duty analog tech

The most important thing to know about Bay 12: Mech Repair is that these are mechs of the MechWarrior or possibly Patlabor school – that is, basically WW2 tanks on hydraulic legs, with cockpits full of switches and wireframe displays. Their bodies are assemblages of pistons and reactors. They are not biomechs like the ones in Evangelion. An Evangelion Repair game would be… different. Less industrial, more Oedipal. You would dread removing the smallest piece of housing.

Which isn't to say that Bay 12: Mech Repair represents life on Easy Street, exactly. There's a big war happening outside, its fortunes palpable in the minced leg joints and pocked torsos of the war-bots lowered into your hangar. You're also fed details about the lives of pilots when you accept a work order. Lieutenant Iona Vale of the 3rd Recon Company says there's "left leg hesitation after extended operation", especially at higher temperatures. That sure sounds like a thing that could get Lieutenant Iona Vale killed.

It's not clear whether you can diagnose faults incorrectly, and shape the progress of the conflict, but the context brings extra emotional charge to what might otherwise be a cosy process of glueing together very expensive Air-Fix models, for all the sense of scale.

Bay 12: Mech Repair follows a familiar flow, as job sims go. Banged-up Iron Giants arrive in a steady procession. You figure out what's wrong with them based on scans, pilot reports, and so forth. Then you get out there with a welder, drill and spanner to make it right. Busted parts can be salvaged for scrap for custom components. Completed work orders net you credits that must be divided between restocking your inventory and buying new tools.

You also have the option of clearing away rust and applying a new paintjob. I'm fascinated to know if this has any real impact on either the story or your fortunes, because I guarantee that I am going to spend far more time obsessing over dazzle camouflage than giving the ol' actuators a haircut.

Read more on Steam. The devs, Crimson Herring Studios, are them wot did Sovereign Syndicate, an apparently decent Victorian fantasy RPG that we never found time to review. Look, I am not made of thumbs and eyeballs. As for the daunting possibility of an Evangelion Fixing Sim, the recently announced Valkyrie Iteration gets into some of the squirming detail, there.

#3885. GOTY hopeful Mina the Hollower bought the studio financial stability "for now," while the Shovel Knight devs work on a new 3D game

Yacht Club Games has confirmed that most of its developers are now working on a brand new 3D game (potentially Shovel Knight 3D), after the critically-acclaimed Mina the Hollower did well enough for the team to continue.

Before launching its old-school adventure game earlier this year, Yacht Club described Mina the Hollower as a "make-or-break" moment for the beloved indie studio. A global pandemic and a failed experiment to turn Yacht Club into a multi-project studio had left the developer on thin ice, it seems.

But Mina the Hollower sold well enough to buy the studio more time, according to a new Reddit AMA full of interesting tidbits. Asked if Mina was able to secure financial stability for the company, Sean Velasco simply said "yes… for now!" Mina managed to sell over 500,000 copies in its first two weeks, so it's well on its way to the one million copies the devs were once hoping for.

For the foreseeable future, the devs aren't ready to talk about the kinds of DLC and spin-offs and follow-ups that dear old Shovel Knight enjoyed for many years, but they're not abandoning their newest baby either. "We're working on more post-release features," the devs wrote, which includes "expanded randomizer options, enemy and boss randomization, more modifiers, speedrunner features" and more ways "to do even more in Mina."

Another fan also asked the folks at Yacht Club about their unannounced 3D Shovel Knight game - Velasco previously told Bloomberg that the game was halfway done before the entire studio put all hands on deck for Mina, and pivoted back into a one-game outfit. Alec Faulkner stopped short of confirming Shovel Knight 3D, but said "most of us are currently working on a 3D game, yes!" Alright then, Alec, keep your secrets. "Not sayin more! Other than that it’s gonna be soooooooo awesome."

Co-founder Nick Wozniac went further into the state of the developer, and why splitting the team in half was probably a mistake. Here's what he had to say on the matter: "Sales are the things that keep the company afloat so it's not born from greed (mostly) that we say we'd love to see more sales, it's all about continuing to work together and make great games and reaping the rewards along the way. We are doing ok and learned a lot this cycle. I think we learned mostly that keeping the team tight and focused is what helped Mina land. Splitting the team up to work on two games was something we could have corrected a long time ago but I'm glad to be where we are now. Just gotta pocket those lessons and use them to drive you forward."

Eurogamer's five-star Mina the Hollower review called it an "adventure that takes inspiration from the greats."

#3883. You can make a vampire hunter who's afraid of the dark, disease and small spaces in Hunter: The Reckoning - Deathwish, and that's surely the best way to play

A month or two back I penned a 1500 word whine about feeling too powerful in Blood of Dawnwalker. "Gimme a vampire sim in which I'm a pathetic vein-nibbling goblin," I wrote, using many more adjectives than that. Well, never let it be said that I'm biased against vampires, for I am equally keen to play an RPG in which I am the least capable vampire hunter in the universe. A vampire hunter who screams when he wakes up with his hair over his face. A vampire hunter who has to spray the vampires with antibac before staking them.

An RPG like Hunter: The Reckoning – Deathwish, perhaps, which presents you with a choice of Advantages and Flaws when creating a character. You have to balance these out on a gnarly weighing scale, before they'll let you through the game's front door. Here is a video showing all that off, together with a lot of sixpacks.

The Advantage/Flaw system looks familiar on the surface. Advantages include Warrior, which gives you +15% chance of a critical hit, or Charmer, which gives you a +1 to Persuasion skill checks. Flaws include clumsy, bad reputation, fear of darkness, hypochondriac, and claustrophobia.

I don't know much about the tabletop game on which Deathwish is based, and the video skims the detail here, but I suspect the last three Flaws will boil down to something like "-1 Constitution in Unlit Closets". Still, I really enjoy the idiocy of going up against crypt-dwelling undead while being unable to tolerate shadows, small spaces, and disease. In general, I'd love it if Hunter: The Reckoning – Deathwish steered well away from any possibility of simply overpowering the vamps, to say nothing of the werewolves and other creatures of the night.

This appears to be the idea: devs Teyon have stressed their desire to make something more story and investigation-driven, after the stomping gibfest that was RoboCop: Rogue City. As narrative designer Mateusz Działowski put it in a previous dev diary, they've "switched from action with RPG elements into RPG with action elements". Amongst other things, you'll need to put together a team of fellow would-be slayers, each with secrets and traumas, and gather clues about best tactics while roaming the game's condensed and shiny New York City. You can read more about it all on Steam.

PC Gamer's annual list of the 100 best PC games you can play—updated for 2026

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Welcome to the PC Gamer Top 100—our annual list of the best games you can play right now. Every year, we look at the hundreds of thousands of PC games that are available to buy, and think, "yes, we can whittle this down into a numbered list". Hubris? Yes. A months-long crucible of heated arguments and impassioned pleas? Also yes.

More than anything, the Top 100 is designed to capture a moment in time. It's a place where the 'canon' classics of the past rub shoulders against the fresh new hotness. Where being a game that a significant portion of the team currently loves is as important as being a game that is recognised worldwide for its contributions to the medium.

It is a deeply subjective process—a way for PC Gamer's editorial team to advocate for the games they're passionate about. One member of our team has spent years attempting to get Overwatch back on the list, taking every opportunity to persuade their fellow editors to give it a chance. Not every entry required that level of dedication to earn its spot, but every pick is a game that at least a handful of our staff cares deeply about.

Ahead of the vote, the PC Gamer team is free to nominate any PC game for voting, giving us a longlist of over 300 games. Each member of the team is then asked to rate those games subjectively across three weighted categories:

The weightings are designed around the Top 100's function as an annual, ever-changing list. Too much weight to Importance, and the list stagnates. Too much to Freshness, and there's no consistency year-to-year. Quality is the most important category because, ultimately, if we don't think a game is actually very good, it doesn't make the list.

The sum of each game's ratings is divided by its number of voters, and then run through a few special formulae—including a penalty for games that receive too few votes—to produce the final Top 100 Score for each game.

We then make some manual adjustments. In the interest of variety we mostly restrict the list to one game per series—only including multiple if we think the games are different enough from each other to be worth mentioning, as with Baldur's Gate 2 and Baldur's Gate 3. Otherwise, the lower scoring game in a series is removed. We also let editors pitch for a change to the list—each of which is voted on by the wider team, and only ratified if it gets majority approval.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

What's left is the 100 games you find below. Some might claim it folly—attempting to wrestle the varied tastes of our editorial team into a list of games we wholeheartedly recommend. Nevertheless, we're sure that within these entries, you'll find something new to love.

Elie Gould: I'm in no way a MOBA-lover but I sure do love Deadlock. I love its fantastically written characters, exciting and experimental game design, and its mode for dummies: Street Brawl.

Jacob Ridley: Welp, Elie has called me out. I play Deadlock for dummies, otherwise known as Street Brawl, and it's something special. A large cast of otherworldly characters keeps every round fresh. It's surprisingly accessible through excellent character, UI, and game design—a high skill ceiling, but fun all the way down. Great game, and I'm yet to even try the MOBA mode.

Elie Gould: That wasn't a call out, Jacob. I also love and play Deadlock for dummies, it rocks!

Andrea Shearon: It's me, the MOBA-lover logging in to say I've only put a handful of hours into Deadlock and already love it. I'm the reverse of Elie and not into hero shooters, but Deadlock (and Calico) have won me over.

Harvey Randall: It's also me, the person on the PC Gamer team with 360+ hours in this thing—and while I do (unfortunately, it's a character flaw) know how to play MOBAs, Deadlock is shaping up to be the best-in-class of the entire genre. Which means, as my fellows have stated, it also has an absolute ton going for it outside of just being a very good example of itself.

Valve has cooked up one of its coolest settings—a supernatural 1950s New York where barrel mimics lurk on street corners and Lovecraftian gods play at their own versions of the Grand Budapest. And while it's not yet finished, the fact it's getting record-high concurrents should tell you just how much Valve has cooked here.

Jake Tucker: I've tried and failed to get into Deadlock a few times now, and the main draw is the incredible world. MOBAs could be accused, usually, of being a little bit of a fantasy hodgepodge, but Deadlock's setting is consistent and fascinating, a tiny city for you to explore each game.

Released: March 19, 2026 | Top 100 Score: 215.31

Morgan Park: I consider Death Stranding 2 the perfect kind of sequel. It builds on all of the fantastic hiking, delivery, and construction stuff that ruled about the original while rethinking what kinda sucked (combat). The addition of proper bandit camps and expanded combat options really rounds out its sandbox into something special—a contemplative walking simulator, a complex logistics game, and a memorable immersive sim. The first Death Stranding is one of my favorites, but On The Beach upstages it on all fronts. Personally, it should rate higher.

Sean Martin: Death Stranding 2 has a similar magic to Control, but where that game juxtaposes the mundanity of office life with paranormal occurrences, Death Stranding 2 actually makes logistics work ridiculously fun. I built a little truck, slapped as many batteries to the outside as I could, and drove it across Australia, even through Timefall events, which is more than any delivery man should have to deal with.

Issy van der Velde: Like all great sci-fi, Citizen Sleeper uses its futuristic setting to explore a very current problem. Trapped on derelict space station the Eye and caught between a corrupt trade union, gang, and your former corporate owners, you play as a Sleeper whose mind has been digitised and put into a decaying robot body. The expensive stabilizer needed to keep from falling apart can easily be swapped for numerous real-world analogs: insulin, inhalers, hormones, antidepressants, even food and water. The fact that the need for stabilizer is the result of planned obsolescence only makes the game's parallels to our present day even more conspicuous.

I managed to carve out a nice life on the Eye despite the horrors of capitalism, and maybe that's the point—you may not change the whole world, but you can change yours.

Harvey Randall: Citizen Sleeper is one of those games that caught me at a very important time in my life—new job, new city, and big, scary changes. Morrowind is a rich, textured, and singular meal that you can't get anywhere else, heavy on the mushrooms and redolent with exotic and alien spices—and you bet it's still delicious as hell, even in 2026.

Andy Chalk: It makes me a little sad to know that Bethesda will never make another game like Morrowind, because Bethesda is now a cog in a machine whose primary function is safety. But in the early 2000s? Man, they were going for it. Sure would like a remaster of that.

Sean Martin: I love Morrowind as much as the next gamer—it was the first Elder Scrolls game I touched when I was but small and it had an effect much like cocaine on my young impressionable mind. But in the year of our lord 2026 are we finally going to admit the combat has aged horrendously?

Jody Macgregor: No one liked the combat even when Morrowind was new. We just didn't care.

Joshua Wolens: The problem with kids today [Josh and Sean were born the same year –Ed] is they don't want to struggle for anything. Is Morrowind's combat a ceaseless, grinding nightmare in its early hours? Yes, but so is life. And then you get better, your numbers go up, and you begin to understand the systems, and the late-game highs that come with being able to make mincemeat of anyone and everyone with your ridiculously overpowered build are dizzying. It just wouldn't be the same if you didn't spend a few hours failing to hit anyone at first.

Sean Martin: You're right. I blame our culture of instant gratification.

Released: August 24, 2012 | Top 100 Score: 244.86

James Bentley: Dark Souls, FromSoft's brooding fantasy RPG, has an impeccable tone, some wonderfully cyclical writing, and a soundtrack that nearly earns the spot by itself. Every now and then, I find myself thinking through the tragic story of Catarina, or Lautrec's ring, or Solaire's reason for pushing on despite the encroaching dark, and realise how deep this game has got its claws into my psyche. And I'm happily trapped in its abyss.

Sean Martin: Check out Dark Souls: Remastered if it's your first time—though lackluster as remasters go, it's still the best way to play.

Harvey Randall: A videogame so inescapable and impactful, the phrase "X is the Dark Souls of Y" became a meme. Dark Souls somehow managed to popularise difficult videogames—a task that, up until its release, seemed impossible. And for its success, we have so many excellent games to enjoy. Not just FromSoft's core library, but all of the imitators and demi-soulslikes that've come since.

Issy van der Velde: Which ending I consider the "good" one changes as I do. Some years, I think carrying on no matter what is the way to go. Others, I believe ushering in a new age is better. Great art grows with you, which is why Dark Souls is so high in our ranking.

Wes Fenlon: The best interconnected map in gaming history and the freeform way in which you can explore it is what keeps Dark Souls near the top of the list year after year. Because let's be honest: Armored Core 6 and Sekiro are way more fun to play moment-to-moment.

Shaun Prescott: Easily the best interconnected map in gaming history, Wes. I can explore it thoroughly in my mind and I've only played through the game twice. One of the most gorgeous and engrossing digital worlds I've ever inhabited and there's no serious competition.

Released: December 5, 2019 | Top 100 Score: 245.13

The landscape is both vast and intricately detailed, ageing like fine wine in the nearly 10 years since launch. And blimey, the music is the cherry on top.

Released: May 30, 2019 | Top 100 Score: 245.71

Sean Martin: Poignant yet playful, this cub scout sci-fi mystery sees you explore an endlessly looping solar system, uncovering the secrets of its quaint yet terrifying planetary dioramas as they fall to entropy around you. Imagine Majora's Mask as a puzzle sandbox and you'll come close to getting a picture, but it's almost impossible to describe Outer Wilds' tonal complexity, juxtaposing, as it does, cozy campfires with the end of all things. It's a game you really need to play to understand, and you should play it.

Released: September 14, 2017 | Top 100 Score: 247.03

Jody Macgregor: The Kickstarter-backed CRPG revival gave us a bunch of enjoyably retro trips back to Top-Down Town like Pillars of Eternity, but Divinity: Original Sin 2 combined that nostalgia with actual forward momentum.

It mattered which of your companions you controlled while talking to NPCs, not just because of their score in the Persuasion skill but because of who they were and how they fit into the world. Plus, while almost everyone else was trying to revive realtime-with-pause combat, Larian found new space to evolve turn-based tactics and elemental damage types.

I can't think of another game that says, sure, blood is wet, of course you can use it to put out fires and conduct electricity, and that's going to matter once you figure out how to produce the stuff in truly industrial quantities.

Harvey Randall: I love DoS2, but boy am I glad that Larian decided to tone down the surfaces for Baldur's Gate 3. And I am slightly worried we'll be returning to the same screen-flooded environmental spam with the upcoming Divinity. But hey, setting an entire field of flammable ground into a scorching hellscape is a good time, and I've no qualms about DoS2 being here on this list.

Wes Fenlon: While Baldur's Gate 3 feels like a straight improvement in so many ways, the origin stories in DoS2 are still incredibly strong. Even playing through it over the course of six months in a chaotic co-op group, my character Lohse's story ended up one of my favorites in any RPG.

Released: November 16, 2004 | Top 100 Score: 249.24

A fool might tell you that this game is old fashioned, out of date, maybe even surpassed. I wish that was true, because here 22 years after its release, there's still nothing else like it.

Sean Martin: You're not really a PC gamer until you've killed a headcrab with a crowbar. I don't make the rules!

Released: December 10, 1993 | Top 100 Score: 250.21

Doom matters in ways that even games like Half-Life 2 don't, and the fact that you can still fire it up and see that significance for yourself is proof of its fundamental greatness.

Jody Macgregor: My favorite part of Doom is the early techbase levels, where the most complicated thing that is likely to happen is that you'll see a tease of an outdoor area, only to arrive at it later on. Eventually the teleporters show up and it becomes a game of navigating labyrinths while flipping switches and juggling keys, but Doom at its best is pure and primal, a cave-painting of a videogame where the cavemen have only just discovered the color red.

Wes Fenlon: You guys heard of the new hotness, Doom 2? Why settle for a single shotgun when you can have both barrels?

Fraser Brown: Murder your cousin! Eat your uncle! Declare all the wars! I don't know why I'm shouting! I can't help but become irritatingly enthusiastic about Crusader Kings 3—the pinnacle of Paradox Development Studio's experiments in combining grand strategy with roleplaying.

Lincoln Carpenter: CK3 is like participating in a multigenerational murder mystery dinner, but there's at least as many additional murders in progress as there are participants, there's a religious war for Bohemia going on upstairs, and the building's going to catch on fire when the Holy Roman Empire collapses. But in a fun way.

Joshua Wolens: With repeated kidnappings, murder plots against family members, and myriad invasions, I once made a rival's life such a living hell in CK3 that I began feeling genuinely bad about it in reality.

Released: February 4, 2016 | Top 100 Score: 251.90

Lincoln Carpenter: There's an incomparable magic to taking a raw, untested recruit, giving him the name of one of your old high school friends, subjecting him to dozens of high-stakes anti-alien guerilla deployments with all the associated battlefield tragedies, devastating misfires, and trauma-bonded comrades they entail, and watching him gradually become the last, best hope of a subjugated humanity who just so happens to have a retroengineered xenotech shotgun that can punch a hole clean through whatever is the closest approximation the Advent have for God.

Fraser Brown: Still the best tactics game, hands down. This year I grew to appreciate it even more thanks to Zero Company. It has all of the ingredients of XCOM 2, but it just did nothing for me. That's because Firaxis worked some real magic with this one. It's properly special. I have nothing bad to say about it, which is incredibly rare for me.

Harvey Randall: You know how people will often take their roombas in for repairs, rather than exchanging them for a new model, because they've become attached to them? Released: February 26, 2016 | Top 100 Score: 252.83

Lauren Morton: The game that invented farm sims—just kidding, but "the game that reminded us how good Harvest Moon was" doesn't really roll off the tongue. Is my fear that the years will flee from me, paradoxically, the only thing that ensures they will?

Shaun Prescott: My kids have played Stardew Valley for most of their childhood, so its soundtrack has flooded my house on Saturday and Sunday afternoons for years. It's genuinely gorgeous stuff. That Eric Barone composed it all on his lonesome is endlessly impressive.

Elie Gould: I frickin love this little blocky game. I only get the urge to play Minecraft every six months or so now, but those few weeks are always full of the best times—whether that be working on my expanding underground dwarven city or in my friend's Skyblock server where I'm forced to farm dirt.

You can add furniture because Mojang oddly refuses too (I'm not mad), turn it into a Souls-inspired RPG, or make it a factory automation game. It's timeless. Like Skyrim, I'll always get the annual urge to return to it.

Sean Martin: What if Dark Souls embraced the open world formula? It's a simple concept, but Elden Ring stands testament to how successfully it was realised. Take FromSoft's iconic combat, boss fights, and quests, then explode them into an enigmatic world you slowly explore and unravel. I have over 800 hours in Elden Ring (plus 500 in Nightreign) and I still started a new playthrough when Tarnished Edition released.

Andy Chalk: I don't like Souls games but I loved Elden Ring, because it let me avoid the whole Souls thing: Instead of all that dodge-parry-slash nonsense (and no offense if that's what you're into, but brother, I am not), I just gave myself a big brain with a big stick, and melted everything. Some fans of the genre might say I deprived myself of the 'real' Souls experience, but I got to enjoy one of the most stunning fantasy worlds I've ever explored—something I'd have missed if the game hadn't been willing to let me play it on my own terms.

Harvey Randall: I have played Elden Ring (and its expansion) exactly once, and I will admit, I've not had the stomach to do so a second time—the scope of these games is a touch overwhelming to me. But that one playthrough did utterly enthral and capture me, so I can't complain too much. Besides, Sean plays enough Elden Ring for all of us.

Issy van der Velde: Elden Ring is the antithesis of the focus found in Sekiro, and it still rules. I love that Andy could have fun melting everyone while I got to enjoy shredding them with a big spikey wheel axe.

Released: May 18, 2015 | Top 100 Score: 258.38

Ted Litchfield: I was late to the party (maybe not so much in the grand scheme) getting The Witcher 3 for Christmas in 2015. Velen is great, but things really clicked for me in Novigrad. One of my fondest gaming memories remains sitting on a beanbag in my parents' basement over the break, my chunky, already-aging laptop plugged into the TV with its fans screaming. I was rocking a first gen, owl-faced Steam Controller, and I was so invested in the search for Sigi Reuven's treasure that I pulled an all-nighter by accident.

11 years on, The Witcher 3 is still, somehow, one of the best-looking videogames out there, its balance of art direction and photorealism gracefully aging like a DILF-y Hollywood leading man. I think CDPR has managed to at least match the achievement of The Witcher 3 with Cyberpunk, but that's hardly a universal opinion, and Geralt's final(?) outing remains a triumph.

Jody Macregor: I do think The Witcher 3 has a magic Cyberpunk 2077 didn't match. The way it's structured incentivises pushing on in your search for Yennefer and then Ciri without feeling like you have such limited time you can't engage with whichever of its many excellent sidequests catches your interest. There's just enough impetus to keep up the momentum without making you feel like it's out-of-character to have a little fun. And if you crank the difficulty up Geralt's combat style (prep-heavy research-based battle herbalism) is actually great.

Andy Chalk: One of my favorite things about The Witcher 3 (and spoiler here, but it's been a decade) is that when all is said and done—if you played your cards reasonably right—Geralt gets a happy ending. I like happy endings, and if any videogame guy deserves one, it's Geralt. That dude powered through some shit, and as much as I'd like his adventures to continue, the send-off CD Projekt gave him with Blood and Wine left me far happier to call it done.

Joshua Wolens: Geralt of Rivia will return in The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past, and so help me CDPR if you do anything bad to him I'm picketing your offices.

Andy Chalk: Yeah, just a little follow-up to my previous comment here: If CD Projekt does a Vesemir to Geralt, I am gonna be setting shit on fire.

Released: October 15, 2019 | Top 100 Score: 259.74

Ted Litchfield: Disco Elysium was the game that made me get serious about a career in games. It's now one of the biggest bummers I have to deal with professionally. The IP ownership and financial allegations? Byzantine. The interpersonal strife among its developers? Distressing. The layoffs and lives upended in its wake? To quote my man Geralt of Rivia, Poland's most soulful white boy from the previous entry on this list: It's "the last bitter drop in a chalice of sorrow."

And yet. Cut to the game underneath it all, and you'll still find a potentially life-changing work of baffling, miraculous provenance. Punks don't know how to make each other do the dishes without a struggle session. How the fuck did they make a game?

Six years on, it's easy to take Disco's design innovations for granted: Strip the so-so combat out of Planescape: Torment and replace it with a union of RPG and point 'n click adventure. Dialogue windows in the bottom-center of the screen with walls of text suck, so hammer it into a much more parsable, right-oriented vertical feed instead. Have the skills you invest in not only open opportunities, but shift the tone of the experience with their distinctive, hallucinatory personalities.

Disco tells a story with heart and characters that feel real, set in a tiny slice of a world that blends alternate history with pure fantasy like the best 20th century sci-fi writers, your Le Guins, Herberts, and Dicks. Its authors were people of strong social and political conviction who nevertheless trusted players enough to let them disagree and take the story in wildly different directions without it feeling like a failure state.

As I grow older, I've become more partial to stories that end. But we didn't get our fill of Elysium, and I still hope we can go back, someday.

Fraser Brown: A lot of the writing around Disco focuses on how weird it is, or how wonderful it is to have a videogame that's actually funny, and all of those things are true. But what really sticks with me is how heartbreaking it is. It's one of the only videogames to ever make my eyes get a bit leaky. Underneath all the high concept weirdness and political orienteering, it's an incredibly human game that hits like a fucking truck. We'll never see its like again.

Phil Savage: Heartbreaking, yes, but also hopeful. That's the thing that I wasn't expecting when I finally played it earlier this year. Not hopeful in an "everything's going to be OK" kind of way, Disco's optimism is both smaller and grander than that. Everything is not going to be OK, and maybe that's OK. Maybe, if you work on yourself, you can find some meaning in that. Maybe the arthropods are in silent and meaningless awe of you.

Harvey Randall: While you're distracted thinking about everything said above, I'm going to take this chance to go on record and say that I want to marry Kim Kitsuragi. That is all.

Issy van der Velde: I went into Disco Elysium with high expectations, but what I didn't anticipate was the mirror it would hold up to me. It made me realise I'll always be an addict at heart, but it also reaffirmed my desire to overcome that. I didn't let Harry relapse even though he's only pixels and words. I'm flesh and bone, so surely I deserve even better?

Released: August 3, 2023 | Top 100 Score: 270.30

Fraser Brown: Here we are again. Baldur's Gate 3 is our number one game for another year, and let's face it—it's probably going to be taking this spot again in 2027. It's just so damn impressive. There are few games I can say this about, but if you don't get on with BG3, I don't think we can be friends (just don't tell my partner, who doesn't remotely understand the hype). This is one of the best ever RPG studios firing on all cylinders, building on decades of experience and experiments. I hope RPGs haven't peaked with BG3, but I'm struggling to imagine a future where this doesn't continue to be my favourite game of all time.

Sean Martin: I don't even like Dungeons & Dragons that much, and yet I'm one of only 3% of players who've completed the game in Honour Mode. I'm not even sure how that happened? Baldur's Gate 3 is just so damn enchanting. The prospect of adventure, the wonderfully written characters, and the endless twists and turns your journey takes amount to a truly unique gaming experience. I still consider myself blessed that I got to see the orchestral concert in London where Andrew Wincott appeared and sang Raphael's Final Act, because that song is an all-timer.

Jody Macgregor: The Forgotten Realms isn't always an interesting backdrop for roleplaying, and I say that as someone who has run multiple campaigns there. Larian turned it into one by making the obligatory Realms stuff a delight—Volo the travelling disaster, Elminster the cheese freak—and pulling in cool bits from other D&D settings like githyanki and illithids so the world feels slightly alien and part of a larger cosmology. BG3 is a fantasy RPG through and through, but one that restores some of the genre's sense of wonder.

The thing that really makes it special is the reactivity. Act 3 is constantly referencing stuff you did in Act 1, and I only just found out if you take over the newspaper you can print your own stories, changing the city folk's ambient dialogue. Everything you do feels like it matters.

Ted Litchfield: 2023, '24, and much of '25 were dominated by BG3 for me, and it's been a second since I fired it up. I've been on a real Owlcat kick (we'll get Wrath of the Righteous or Rogue Trader on this list next year, prayer warriors), and when my favorite game is no longer right in front of me, my feckless heart can drift. Was it really that good?

Yes. Unequivocally. Universal heavyweight champion of the world. Just thinking about it for this write up has me wanting to roll a new guy⁠—I've never uninstalled, and I don't think I ever will barring force majeure. Larian simultaneously raised the bar on cinematic RPG storytelling while matching the crunchiest classics in depth and complexity. Common sense previously dictated that the two were mutually exclusive, and it feels like CRPGs can finally look forward, not back.

Harvey Randall: I have about 380 hours in this thing. I've completed it twice, once on honour mode, and I got another two extra honour mode playthroughs to Act 3 before I got distracted and left them in the dirt.

I can confidently call it one of the best RPGs that will perhaps ever be made. There's something about the sheer scope of it, the mixture of immersive sim style branching narratives and CRPG goodness that mashes up with professional, glossy production value and fully motion-captured cutscenes.

And while the TTRPG rules lover in me balks at Larian's irreverently-designed magic items which, let's be clear, grab D&D 5e's intended balance and snap it mercilessly over its knee… I'm still very glad they're there. They make the game a min-maxxer's delight.

Currently, I've been roped into an Honor Mode playthrough with Josh, Sean, and Ted, and my Cleric has stumbled onto a build that debuffs everybody just by standing around her. They can attest that I have made some utterly disgusting laugh-noises whenever I knock someone prone with Reverberation just for looking at me funny.

Surprise! There are more than 100 good videogames. Below you'll find a selection of individual recommendations—each a game that a member of the PC Gamer team thinks you should play.

Tyler Wilde, US Editor-in-Chief: Rocket League hasn't evolved much since 2015, but that's because it was already a perfectly-designed competitive team game which no one has yet improved upon. Playing soccer with rocket-powered cars has a high skill ceiling, but great teamwork can trump individual skill, which has led to some of the most exciting underdog wins of my gaming career. I'll be playing when I'm 80 if they don't turn the servers off before then.

John Strike, Senior Art Editor: Big pies. Flat beer. Crazy northeners. Drunk cows. Thank Goodness You’re Here! has it all and then some. This beautiful cartoon-style slapstick romp around the fictional and truly bizarre Yorkshire town of Barnsworth is a must-play for anyone with a soft spot for northern ways. Put your trousers on, grab your net and go and catch those spirit level bubbles!

Elie Gould, News Writer: Oh my god, I forgot to put Silent Hill f on the voting list. This is unforgivable considering how amazing it is and how well it managed to pave the way for the new kind of Silent Hill we're now seeing unfold. Its setting is chilling, mysterious, and cool as all hell, it gives us the best female protagonist I've seen in years, and we're tested with some seriously tricky puzzles and grotesque monsters. It's the whole package.

Christopher Livingston, Senior Editor: After a long absence I finally returned to Rare's open world ocean sandbox this year, and yep, there's still really no other game like it. The beauty of its world and water is still unmatched and there's nowhere else I've found that shares its blend of chill hangout vibes (90%) and humbling PvP nightmare (10%). All you can bring into each session are your skills because there's nothing else to give any pirate an advantage over another. One of a kind.

Rory Norris, Guides Writer: TESO is my most played game of all time, sitting at well over 2,000 hours in the decade since launch. It's an Elder Scrolls game but multiplayer, and it's been carrying the torch while the mainline series has been radio silent since Skyrim. You can explore almost all of Tamriel at this point, questing, doing world bosses, dungeons, and whatnot. And while it's technically a bit of a mess, the large-scale PvP is truly a sight to behold.

Ted Litchfield, Associate Editor: This one was supposed to be on the list proper, sorry everyone. Deadlock, I love you sweetie, but you're not finished. Step aside for what will be PCG's 2026 RPG of the year barring a coup and my execution. Esoteric Ebb riffs on Disco Elysium, but meaningfully pushes the evolving subgenre forward with smart changes like 6 attributes instead of 24 skills, potentially even greater reactivity⁠—especially in its handwritten turn-based battles⁠—and a comedic, hopeful, tone to set its excellent story apart.

Jody Macgregor, Weekend Editor: I may be a turn-based lover who sometimes thinks we should add Jagged Alliance to the Top 100, but even I know there have been a couple of classic RTSes, chief among them Dawn of War. It's got the best sense of scale of any game in the genre, a real feeling of ants versus bison as you build up to tanks and daemons, and the Definitive Edition lets you pull the camera back to appreciate it. Good luck, ants.

Joshua Wolens, News Writer: A 2024 narrative adventure that's more or less a visual novel, 1000xResist is one of those games that make you realise how narratively unambitious most other videogames are. It's about killing god, doing a revolution, inheriting trauma, inflicting trauma, the immigrant experience, the Hong Kong protests, original sin, noodles, and a lot else. It's like a modern Planescape: Torment, in that it's so tenderly and confidently written that it just makes all the other guys look bad.

Evan Lahti, Strategic Director: If you're an XCOM person with any affection for '80s/'90s action movies, JA3 should be your next game. It's campy, it's tropical, and your mercenaries (through story or tactical decisions) can find themselves in no-win scenarios. But my favorite detail is the simmy ballistics: bullets aren't just particle effects, they're physical objects that can scatter randomly and catch collateral hits against enemies, friendlies, civs, or scenery. The campaign itself is delightfully tabletop in its combo of scripted stuff and freedom.

Issy van der Velde, Deputy Editor, PC Gaming Show: Transistor has the best sci-fi love story I've ever experienced, and the combat is endlessly satisfying. Each ability can be used on its own, added to another to create a secondary effect, or held as a passive buff. It's easy to see how Supergiant built on this to create the boons in Hades. Everyone should play this masterpiece for Ashley Barrett and Darren Korb's soundtrack alone. There's even a dedicated button that lets you hum along to the music.

Phil Savage, Global Editor-in-Chief: If you like the idea of Blue Prince, but don't like the roguelike elements, then I have two things to tell you: 1) You are weak and need to fix yourself, and 2) you should play Lorelei and the Laser Eyes. Simogo's mystery box adventure is an absolute treat of puzzle design, cleverly laying out its challenges in cascading threads of discovery. It's deeply satisfying to solve both the individual puzzles and the building mystery of its story. A genuine treat.

Andy Chalk, US News Lead: The Plants vs. Zombies remaster that dropped in 2025 took some heat for technical shortcomings and allegations of AI art, but EA's addressed most of the complaints and these days it stands as a really good remaster of an all-time classic. The original is still available too, and much cheaper, and it holds up remarkably well for its age. Either way, Plants vs. Zombies is a short, snappy, incredibly cute and easy-to-engage tower defense game that remains as great—and essential—as ever.

Sean Martin, Senior Guides Writer: I'm unsure why my compatriots turned on Total War this year, but I'm here to remind you that Three Kingdoms is still incredible. Its quality is often overshadowed by its early demise, but it's quite unlike anything Creative Assembly ever made, or will likely make again. It channels the courageous characters, political machinations, and endless scheming of China's most culturally iconic period into a top-tier strategy game, achieving a harmonious balance between history and romance.

Andrea Shearon, Evergreen Writer: I've been enjoying the survival crafting renaissance, and by that I mean playing the hell out of Abiotic Factor and Enshrouded. The unbelievably detailed, massive high-fantasy RPG has one of the best building systems I've ever seen, and I love rescuing new villagers and crafters to slowly grow my own town. My only complaint is that Embervale is so pretty that I spend dozens of hours whispering, "Oh, maybe I'll settle down here," without getting anything done.

Morgan Park, Staff Writer: A gritty, unforgiving rally racing sim set in outer space. Exo Rally takes an already challenging rally format and adds gravity and thrusters into the mix. You'll tear your hair out trying to complete a singular turn on the moon, then ride the high of circumventing most of a track through well-timed thruster use. I haven't played enough yet to make my case for on the list, but it's turning me into a racing fan. A brilliant 2026 indie that's flying too low under the radar.

Mollie Taylor, Features Producer: I'm 13 years late to the party, but Project Zomboid's brutal, complex, and ridiculously moreish take on zombie survival has gripped me this year. It's one of the most customisable sandbox games I've ever tinkered with, meaning you can go for an unforgiving post-apocalyptic landscape or fine-tune it into a cosy (if not slightly gritty and terrifying) zombified The Sims 1. One of the few games I've been happy to sink hundreds of hours into learning.

Jacob Ridley, Managing Editor, Hardware: There are some games you can sink hour after hour into and not even realise it's already morning. Valheim is one of those games. Jump in with a couple of friends and build a new homestead, trying to one-up each other with ever more elaborate creations (our Sistine Chapel are two rival towers on top of massive rocks). Or just go exploring and hunt for new lands, hoping to survive the treacherous ocean journey. Yeah, it's a comfort game for me.

Andy Edser, Hardware Writer: Crimson Desert is not the ultimate action RPG, despite wearing the ambition proudly on its sleeve. But it's also the most fun I've had in a fantasy open world in years. The map is gigantic, and stuffed with bizarre details to explore. The combat is fiddly, yet satisfying to master. It's a game with obvious passion running underneath it, and a brilliant, bat-swinging attempt to make something with real scope and fresh ideas. More of this sort of thing, please.

Harvey Randall, Staff Writer: Perhaps a bit of a late entrant to catch PC Gamer's eye—which means I don't resent its absence from our Top 100 list—but I absolutely loved Mina the Hollower. It's a sprawling, satisfying Zelda-like with a bumping soundtrack and some of the best exploration I've had in a videogame. I was particularly impressed by how intuitive this game was. My experimentation-loving brain was constantly rewarded for putting its control scheme together in novel ways. Cute little mouse versus the eldritch horrors, what's not to love.

Fraser Brown, Online Editor: Big Walk launched after we created the magazine version of the Top 100 this year, otherwise I know it would have been in the list. This is simply the perfect co-op game. A simple, joyful puzzler absent a single flaw. Some of the antics its puzzles inspired genuinely left my crying with laughter, and that ending? Wow. It's a pure delight, start to finish. It's easily going to be my GOTY for 2026.

Phil has been writing for PC Gamer for nearly a decade, starting out as a freelance writer covering everything from free games to MMOs. He eventually joined full-time as a news writer, before moving to the magazine to review immersive sims, RPGs and Hitman games. Now he leads PC Gamer's UK team, but still sometimes finds the time to write about his ongoing obsessions with Destiny 2, GTA Online and Apex Legends. When he's not levelling up battle passes, he's checking out the latest tactics game or dipping back into Guild Wars 2. He's largely responsible for the whole Tub Geralt thing, but still isn't sorry.

#3881. A former volunteer is threatening legal action against fan-made game project Skyblivion

A former volunteer is threatening legal action against Skyblivion, the long-running fan remake of Oblivion built in Skyrim's engine, over code they contributed to the project.

The unofficial project, which remakes 2006's The Elder Scrolls 4: Oblivion, is being made by volunteers from the TES Renewal Project, the modding group that also works on Morrowind remake Skywind.

Bethesda has allowed the project to continue on condition that it replaces all of the original game's assets, and the team continued working on it after Bethesda released its own Oblivion Remastered in April 2025.

In a statement posted to Twitter/X on 30th October, the Skyblivion team said that after the volunteer left, the two sides disagreed over the "continued use and maintenance" of their work.

A former volunteer is attempting to sue Skyblivion and we need your help pic.twitter.com/3Ee5eQTELG

The main issue was the team's decompilation of parts of that code, which it said was needed "to maintain functionality and fix issues" after its access to the original source code repository was revoked.

According to the team, the volunteer then "escalated to sending legal threats", including demands for the real names and home addresses of its volunteer team leads. The team said this was "something we couldn't accept and think is disproportionate".

The team said it has consulted legal counsel and is "completely confident in our right to maintain the code they submitted". Even so, it said it removed the code "to protect our volunteers from undue stress and ensure a clean break", rebuilding that system from scratch.

Despite this, it says the threats have continued. Its post says the former volunteer is "attempting to sue", but it's not clear whether a lawsuit has actually been filed. The volunteer has not been named.

"Please don't make this a witch-hunt," the team told fans, adding that it wishes the former volunteer "the very best" and hopes to "get this resolved as soon as possible and get on with our planned release of Skyblivion".

Last December, the team delayed Skyblivion from 2025 into 2026.

Revisiting other entries seems to be on the cards, just don't hold your breathe

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Now that Final Fantasy 7 Revelation is coming up, the question is what Square Enix focuses on next. Will we see more remakes, or a return to newer ideas and games? A producer on the franchise believes the latter, unless there's an opportunity to do something special.

In an interview with IGN, Yoshinori Kitase, a higher-up at Square Enix, director of Final Fantasy 7 and producer on the remake trilogy, speaks about the philosophy currently guiding the developer and publisher. "I think that mainly, we are more likely to invest in new titles and new games," he says.

"But at the same time, for example, this time with the [Final Fantasy 7] remake, there were me and other creators who worked on the original game, which we had really strong feelings towards," he adds.

Indeed, one of the strengths of this trilogy is that you have devs who were there the first time and newer creatives involved, all helping to rejuvenate the 1997 classic.

In terms of remaking any installment, 7 always seemed worthwhile. It's extremely well-regarded, but the original could be off-putting to newer players because of its slower pacing. Kitase mentions that specifically, and says Square Enix remains open to such opportunities on a case-by-case basis.

"We really wanted to create something new related to the old game to allow new users to play and to know the appeal of this game as much as the old users who play the old game," he states. "So there might be different cases like this one where the company is willing to invest in remaking old projects and other kinds of games like it happened this time."

A remake of Final Fantasy 9 was apparently happening until this past summer, when reports emerged that the project was now languishing for whatever reason. I could see 8 and 9 getting revisited some day, in a similar fashion to 7, but I suspect management wants to resist turning Final Fantasy, and the company in general, into pure nostalgia bait. In light of these comments, I imagine Final Fantasy 17 is more likely to be revealed before, say, a remake of Final Fantasy 6. Would I be too greedy to ask for both?

#3879. itch.io will soon let you filter games with genAI disclosures out of your search results on the site, after admitting it was previously "critically lacking"

itch.io has unfortunately, much like Steam, long had an issue with genAI content being uploaded in droves, drowning out perfectly good games made by human hands. The apparent standard method against this, voluntary genAI disclosure, has been itch's primary tool to combat this wave of low-quality slop, but hasn't worked out too well; itch revealed a few days ago that 'the number of game pages being created per-day has doubled in the past two months'. Now, in attempts to further combat this, beyond just game assets requiring a genAI disclosure to upload as they have for two years, itch will be expanding the mandatory disclosure to tabletop games, books, comics, and soundtracks, as well as adding a 'no AI' filter directly into the search function.

itch noted in this announcement that its previous moderation of genAI use in projects had been "critically lacking", presumably referring to the unfathomable exponential increase in games being uploaded in the past few months by people who don't give a fuck about creating anything themselves and happily contribute to the death of the planet. itch went on to post "Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop" which, I mean, sure, cool! And, look, as many, many people in itch's replies have pointed out, this is not the same as outright banning AI.

Unfortunately, my question at that point becomes: how? itch is not Steam, not a storefront backed by a gigantic corporation with support staff and quality assurance (which, you know, hasn't helped Steam much either). itch is one full-time employee with several contractors and volunteers. If there is a site-wide ban on genAI, people who use genAI will just start lying and sneaking it into their projects anyway. So, then, users just report the offenders, surely? This then requires a manual verification system, which, as is suggested by the sheer amount of games being uploaded every day, is just not feasible, let alone for a team as small as itch. And, frankly, I don't have a better solution here! This is fucked! What itch is doing is, currently, kinda the best it can right now?

itch is a beautiful thing that allows for people who just want to start making games, making art, making music, making books, to have a free space to share it with the world, and gain eyes on their work as well as necessary feedback to improve. It's less of a store and more of a forum for creators and self-published games to interact, guide one another to new, niche, cool shit. Hell, I made a visual novel and posted it on there, becoming another one of those millions of people for whom itch is a valuable platform for first creations. To have this vital space on a path to ruin as a result of the same vile tech that is also on the verge of pushing the global economy over a cliff due to its creators being caught in their multi-year lies is not a future I hope for itch. This is a step in the right direction, and one I genuinely hope pans out well for it in the long run.

The long-awaited title of the next Elder Scrolls game was revealed in a video marking Bethesda Softworks' 40th anniversary.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Eight years after it was announced, it's finally officially official: The next RPG in Bethesda's long-running Elder Scrolls series is called Sentinel.

The title was revealed in a video celebrating Bethesda's 40th anniversary, narrated by Todd Howard (of course), who cast back to the studio's first game, Gridiron—Bethesda was big on sports games back in the day—before moving into The Elder Scrolls series, the games that would take it to the big leagues, in the early 1990s.

"As we're here in the 40th anniversary, we think about all of the games we've made," Howard says as the video draws to an end.

"And so even though yes, we're looking back,we're also looking forward to all we're doing, particularly with the Fallout franchise and obviously The Elder Scrolls. You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6. And we thought, hey, given the moment, what a perfect time to tell you what The Elder Scrolls 6 is actually called."

And thus is the title revealed: Sentinel.

There's an interesting quote after the title is revealed: "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate." Those words were uttered by Yazar, Moth Priest of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell in the year 4E 206, which was UESP pointed out puts Sentinel at least five years after the events of Skyrim.

No other details are revealed, but the title (and that quote) presumably also reveals the setting: Hammerfell, home of the redguards. Sentinel itself is one of Hammerfell's major kingdoms and capital of the Alik'r Desert—reflected in the teaser's sandy backdrop. It's something of a geographical shift from the flyover of the generic mountains seen in that 2018 reveal, although the Alik'r is bordered by the Dragontail Mountains, so who knows.

So there you have it! The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. Hopefully it won't take another eight years before we hear anything more about it.

#3877. "There’s always a night when Rome burns": South Of Midnight director says that Xbox funding it was "unsustainable", at least in hindsight

"I didn’t know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it"

Compulsion Games parted ways with former owners Xbox, having landed on the long list of things Microsoft were determined to ditch as part of multi-round mass cuts this year. Now, South of Midnight creative director David Sears has suggested that an eventual pulling of the rug was something he feared throughout the game's development, to the point where he seemingly doesn't think he'd have funded it if he'd been in the shoes of Xbox execs.

In an interview with MinnMax, Sears - who left Compulsion in March 2025 - outlined that ideally games big publishers put out aim to fall into one of two buckets. They either make lots of money or increase the prestige of the brand by becoming cultural touchstones across multiple generations. Obviously doing both is the perfect outcome, but Sears pegged South of Midnight as being more geared towards the latter camp. The likes of Double Fine's Keeper and Obsidian's Pentiment are other games which off the top of my head could be said to fit that same mold. The issue, of course, is that when push comes to shove, it's the games which can show a strong bottom line at any given moment which make the best case for their studios' short term survival if cash is tight.

So, South of Midnight lived in a risky place, with Sears recalling: "I literally told people. I was like, yeah, this could be terrible because somebody is going to say, one day, 'The money tap, we're closing those floodgates' and that's going to have really traumatic results downstream". The interviewer then asked Sears if what he was getting at is that, while he's glad Xbox funded South of Midnight, he might not have done so or at least cut the funding earlier if he was in charge of the console maker.

"Yeah, probably," Sears replied. "I mean, I wanted to make it. No doubt. Obviously, because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else's money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah, because I'm not completely selfless. It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable. So, of course, it was going to have a 'shocking' outcome. I mean, it's easy to dissect it now, right? But at the time, I would talk to other directors and [they] would be like, 'How is this happening? I mean, how did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?' And I would always be like, 'For now'. There's always a night when Rome burns and I didn't know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it."

Notably, Sears added that in his view modern Microsoft showed a "more humane" side than the version of the company that existed in the 90s and early 2000s by giving studios like Compulsion a chance to spin out on their own rather than simply shuttering them outright once they were deemed surplus to requirements.

Given the director's no longer at Compulsion, it seems he'll not have a say on what their next game looks like, but as a newly indie studio one would imagine they'll have a keen eye on the bottom line.

#3876. Silent Hill: Townfall adds new Hard difficulty in latest update

Silent Hill: Townfall has added a new Hard difficulty mode and rebalanced every existing setting to make room for it.

The update, patch 1.6.0, went live on PS5, Steam, and the Epic Games Store earlier this week, according to patch notes published by Konami. Konami said the rebalance is designed to create "a smoother difficulty curve for players to choose from".

As part of that rebalance, resources have been adjusted in some sections of the game, and enemies' hearing now gets sharper as the difficulty level goes up. Your position is now visible on the map in whichever mode you pick, while the reduction to the main enemy's attack severity now applies only in Story Mode.

Anyone who picks Nightmare for their first playthrough will now see a warning screen. The difficulty selection menu also gives a clearer summary of how the options differ.

SILENT HILL: TownfallNotice: Game Update (Patch 1.6.0)An update tuning gameplay and addressing some in-game issues is now available.Please check that the version number in the lower right corner of the main menu is displayed as v1.6.155963.*The PlayStation®5 version is…

The update also improves the valve status lighting for colourblind players, adds more hints and tutorials, and tweaks the wording of some puzzle hints and items. The options menu has been reorganised into clearer categories, and the controls remapping option has been renamed to make it clear that keyboard and mouse commands can be remapped there too, not just controllers.

PC players also get a new DLSS Ray Reconstruction option, alongside the usual general improvements and bug fixes.

To check you're on the latest version, look for v1.6.155963 in the lower right corner of the main menu on PC, or v1.6.156035 on PS5.

Developed by Screen Burn and published by Konami, Silent Hill: Townfall launched on PS5 and PC on 24th September. Matt said Townfall showed Silent Hill's "stellar revival continues as new developer Screen Burn melds stealth, meticulous world design, and a dash of social realism for a different sort of survival horror", and awarded it four out of five stars in Eurogamer's Silent Hill: Townfall review.

World of Warcraft's big crossover with Dungeons & Dragons is finally here—and despite being a huge flagship collaboration, one of the biggest MMOs meeting with one of the biggest TTRPGs, I'm sad to say I'm feeling just a touch whelmed. This sourcebook is inconsistent—filled with very cool character options in some places, and just pointing at the already-existing player's handbook in others.

That inconsistency doesn't let the whole project down, mind. There are still some rules tucked away in here that I think are great additions to any campaign, not just a World of Warcraft-themed one.

Let's start with the big one: Classes. WoW and D&D do have a lot of overlap in terms of class fantasy—there's not much in the way of appreciable differences between a Fighter and a Warrior, other than a few iconic abilities being missing from the pack. As a result, this rulebook essentially uses the pre-existing classes as a template to throw some WoW flavour on.

Some of these changes are meaningful—take, for example, the Death Knight. This uses the Paladin's chassis, but throws in a ton of impactful changes, replacing Lay on Hands with Death Coil, for example. It also throws a whole new raft of Death Knight-adjacent spells, adjusts your Find Steed with a cool undead ghost that can phase through objects, and more.

A lot of the classes are solved by custom spells like this—the Paladin, for instance, has just the one new subclass to cover for Holy and a bunch of iconic Paladin spells. But the balance of these is a touch skewiff in places. Take Divine Shield, for instance. This thing is straight busted.

It's a 4th level spell, which does admittedly mean you'll only get it at levels 13 plus, but it makes you immune to not only the damage of a triggering attack, but also all damage until the start of your next turn. AND you can't be moved or have your speed reduced. While absolutely correct for the flavour of WoW's iconic bubble, this is crazy overpowered.

And while some of these classes do have a lot new on offer, others are so thin on content it's a wonder why they're there at all. The rogue gets a particularly short end of the stick, for instance. Outlaw rogues are just given a reskinned version of 5e's Swashbuckler subclass (which does, in fairness, have some new Cunning Strike options to bring it up to parity). Otherwise, the book just points you in the direction of pre-existing subclasses.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Others are a complete miss, too. Shamans are all awkwardly stuffed into the chassis of the Barbarian, which only really works for Enhancement shamans—Elemental and Restoration shamans are pretty much just your standard D&D barbarian with some flavour-adjacent rage options, rather than the full spellcasters they are in the videogame.

This inconsistency in quality applies to character origins, too. Some of them have fully bespoke traits—Dracthyr get their visage forms, Void Elves get this cool void form that triggers when you hit identical numbers on an Advantage/Disadvantage roll, and so on. And then there are Orcs and Dwarves, some of WoW's most iconic races, where the book goes: Just use the stuff that's already in the PHB.

And yet, there's a lot to this supplement I actually like. When it's actually adding new options to the classes, I think they're cool—the Frost Mage flavoured feat, Fingers of Frost, gives you extra cold damage against restrained creatures, for example. But the real thing I would encourage you to just crib for your non-Azerothian games are its gathering and crafting systems.

In 5e (and the 2024 rules), crafting's always been sort of a joke. There are tool proficiencies, but they might come up every once in a blue moon. The actual Player's Handbook just says to half the cost of an item, then smacks you around the head with a massive downtime cost for anything particularly expensive—a suit of plate armor takes a whopping 150 days to craft (though you can split this with extra help). At which point you might as well just eat the GP cost and buy the damn thing.

This book, however, has some really neat rules for gathering and crafting professions. Having the right tool proficiency gives you access to a profession, which you can level up when your proficiency bonus increases to new tiers (which also increases the rarity of the items you can make).

Instead of making players shell out the gold cost, these gathering professions have a neat little table for getting enough golds' worth in raw materials to make the thing, with extra bonuses for beating the involved DC by five or more. When you get to higher levels, certain recipes might require items from specific regions—and you might only know how to make those items via recipes obtained from certain factions.

It's still all pretty lightweight (although each profession does have a useful list of suggested recipes it should know) but that's honestly a boon to this system, rather than a bane, because you could very easily just slot this whole mechanic into your homebrew campaign with very little trouble.

And, more to the point, you could very easily make entire adventure hooks out of going to get specific materials for a recipe here—which helps solve D&D crafting's main issue: It's not relevant unless you have literal months of in-game downtime to kill. While the book doesn't make changes to the time-to-craft issue, it's still a major step up.

The fact that there's plenty to like in this book makes it all the more frustrating that it's so inconsistent."

Renown's another mechanic I like. You get renown with certain factions based on your origins, but you can increase this renown through play to get certain perks. For instance, improved renown with Darnassus gives you the option to learn certain proficiencies, gain a blessing from its leaders, or gather extra materials with herbalism. My favorite of these is the gnomeregan Shield Guardian perk, which specifically states that if you dip below 50 renown again, the guardian turns on you. Sorry buddy, my creator says you dropped off.

Aside from these rules additions, there are also some solid dungeon adventures with their own bespoke stat blocks, extra magic items, and a respectable bestiary full of critters to toss into your campaign.

The fact that there's plenty to like in this book makes it all the more frustrating that it's so inconsistent—some areas have novel, if a little wonky, additions to the system. Others shrug like the book's designers simply ran out of time and budget, pointing towards resources that you already own.

However, if you are looking to run a WoW-specific campaign, or just want crafting rules that don't suck, it very well might be worth checking out on the strength of its secondary mechanics alone. Just don't go in there expecting a 1:1 replication of the MMORPG. This is still Dungeons & Dragons—and in some places, I mean that literally.

Plus Square Enix confirms Final Fantasy 14 has passed 35m registered accounts.

Final Fantasy 14's next expansion, Evercold, will launch on 23rd February 2027, and its second new job is zephyr, a physical ranged DPS that fights with a crossbow and a bird.

Producer and director Naoki Yoshida revealed the job during the opening keynote of the Final Fantasy 14 Fan Festival 2026 in Tokyo. Zephyr pairs crossbow shots with support from an avian familiar called Nephele, and joins Bastion, the greatshield-wielding tank revealed as Evercold's first new job at Fan Festival Berlin earlier this year.

Pre-orders for Evercold and the previously announced Collector's Box open on Wednesday 4th November at 9am GMT. Anyone who pre-orders gets early access, plus a Wind-Up Köttr minion and Halone's Earring, which boosts EXP from defeating enemies by 30 percent. The in-game items are delivered as soon as you pre-order, so you can use the earring to level jobs before Evercold arrives.

The Collector's Box is physical goods only. It doesn't include the game, in-game items or pre-order bonuses. Inside you'll find an art box featuring an Evercold illustration by Yoshitaka Amano, a figure of the Warrior of Light as a reaper, an Ethos metal keychain, a Köttr mini plush, and a Tapestry of the Fourth.

The Square Enix Store is also selling a limited Collector's Bundle that pairs the box with a code for the Digital Collector's Edition on Windows or Mac. Players on PS5, PS4, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2, and Steam can buy the box on its own and pre-order the Digital Collector's Edition separately. The digital edition adds a Valhallar Odin mount, an Entreat Crystal emote, and a Crystal Skyltborg weapon for Bastion.

Square Enix also used the keynote to reveal a new Fierce raid difficulty, sitting between Normal and Savage; a new trailer for the Evangelion: Ghosts of Desire alliance raid crossover, plus tougher eight-player battles built around some of its bosses; and new Tetsuya Nomura artwork for Beyond the Lifestream, a raid series crossover with the Final Fantasy 7 Remake series.

We can also expect Evolved Combat Mode, which Square Enix says highlights each job's unique identity; Seasons, a new system that changes how item rewards are earned; and expanded character creation with new Character Action Skins. Expanded housing features, PvP updates, and a revamped companion chocobo system will follow from patch 8.1.

Final Fantasy 14 has passed 35 million registered accounts.

You can watch the full keynote on Twitch, and there's more on the official Evercold site.

#3870. Arc Raiders devs Embark insist that using genAI for voice lines was necessary, as "actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that"

Despite taking the voice performances of actors and feeding them into machines to spurt out AI-generated mimicry, Embark CCO Stefan Strandberg insists that "we are not in the industry of replacing actors." In a new video posted to the Arc Raiders channel focused on audio design, Strandberg refers back to the infamous use of genAI in Arc Raiders to generate voice lines based on real voice actors' performances, something which the game was heavily (and rightly) criticised for before and since its release.

In that linked piece (thanks Oisin!), CEO Patrick Söderlund stated that they have been replacing lines that were originally generated with actual recorded lines, presumably because Arc Raiders has made quite a bit of money and now they feel that they can continue paying actors to record more lines, rather than just scraping their talents and avoiding the dreaded fee of paying professionals for their work. This choice already came after their previous game, The Finals, was heavily criticised for the exact same thing, which is just a fascinating series of decisions to consider.

In the video, audio director Bence Pajor explains that the apparent reason for the use of AI was to avoid the "stress" of having to work around actors' availability, as they may be busy working on other projects when Embark decides that a new feature needs new voice lines recorded. Pings, quests, and in-level mission briefings were thus generated using training data based on existing actors' recordings, saving the need to actually get anyone back in a studio or pay them for their time. Citing the amount of variables that the ping system creates, Pajor claims it "becomes too impractical to record every possible version of something. The actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that", which is a take that falls apart if you consider the simple fact that games of this scope (or bigger) have been managing to work around actors' availability for as long as genAI has not been an accessible technology, which has been almost all of the time that video games have existed. Isn't it crazy that games like Disco Elysium and Baldur's Gate 3 had so, so much recorded dialogue, all without genAI? Or fellow live service shooter Apex Legends, which has been adding and adjusting voice lines via updates for years? How could they possibly have managed it?

Voice actresses Jo Rideout and Diana Gardner, who play Shani and Celeste respectively, are also featured speaking on their characters' relationships as well as their experience working within this hybrid model of recording and generating voices. Gardner notes that "if they only need an hour of my time for a couple call-outs that are short, then I don't have to cancel other shoots or some other project that might also be interesting. So in that way, I feel quite good about it." She then explains that "the contract seemed fair…so it was a no-brainer in that sense. But I didn't know what to expect once I heard the voice come out. I was like, 'Can I take ownership for the performance?' This is hours of work that I've put in, but can I take ownership for the final product? No."

Strandberg goes on to elaborate on his comment on not replacing actors by saying that "We are not in the industry of replacing actors, actually, I think quite the opposite. We should celebrate the performance, and we should give them more space." While Embark's audio team are indeed working on replacing the generated lines with actual performances, that doesn't change the fact that the choice to use AI in the first place was one made simply to save money in not paying actors for their specific work and get the game out the door faster — effectively the 'we'll fix it in post' of games development. While I can respect Garner's awareness that it means she can prioritise other projects when necessary, there is that notable tinge of regret in not being able to take ownership for her hours of work. Fundamentally, Embark has demonstrated its willingness to cut talent to cut costs, seemingly happy to post PR videos implying they had no choice due to the game's scope, and that isn't something a company just goes back on once they realise how 'efficient' it can be.
